properties.decision: DECIDED by Anthony 2026-08-02, option 3 of three: the sweep is everything the version-control system tracks, minus NAMED exclusions echoed back with the rule that excluded them. No vocabulary change, no new property, no new node type — so the schema stamp does not move, which on this project is what locks out older binaries. (The node id says `declared` because that was the QUESTION; the answer is `derived`. Kept as a stable handle rather than re-minted, since `cap:coverage` is already GOVERNED_BY it.) WHAT IS IN THE REPOSITORY, in his own decomposition — this is the load-bearing part, because getting it wrong is what produced the objection this decision had to overturn. A NON-CODE PROJECT puts TWO things under version control: the reflow2 design graph, and the design artifacts. A CODE PROJECT puts THREE: the reflow2 design graph, the design artifacts, and the actual implemented code. THE FIRST TWO ARE THE CONSTANT. The implemented system is the only term that varies, and it is present in exactly one of the two cases. THE OBJECTION THIS OVERTURNS, which was mine and not his: the weakness recorded against this option said deriving from a repo 'says nothing for a design whose subject is a fleet, a document set, or hardware', against `req:design-anything`. It conflated the SUBJECT SYSTEM with the DESIGN'S ARTIFACTS, and a sweep only ever covers what is in the repository. A satellite, a building, a fleet cannot live in a repo — but its drawings, specs, models, analyses and requirement documents can, and normally do. In his words: 'while a hardware system, for example, can't live within a git repo, its design artifacts can. obviously, for all non-code projects, this is the case.' So a derived scope is not a code-only convenience. It is the general case, and it is MORE clearly right for a non-code project than for software, because there the tracked artifacts are the whole of what a coverage question could ever have been asking about. CODE IS THE SPECIAL CASE, AND SPECIAL BY BEING MORE THAN THE NORM, NOT LESS — 'code based projects are the system and can be inspected by the agent as well as the design'. It is the one case where the third term exists, so one sweep sees the implemented system alongside the graph and the artifacts. He also expects that exceptional case to be the majority of reflow2's use, which is exactly why it must not be mistaken for the rule the design is built on: a default inferred from the common case would quietly assume an implemented system that most subjects do not have. WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THE SWEEP ITSELF. Of the three tracked things, the design GRAPH is the one that must be excluded — a design cannot be its own subject, and `docs/design` is a named exclusion in reflow2's own sweep for exactly that reason. The other two are swept: the artifacts always, the implemented code when there is any. WHAT THIS GENUINELY CANNOT DO, which is a different limitation from the one it was charged with: a design artifact that is NOT under version control — a CAD file on someone's machine, a spec in a wiki, a drawing inside a PLM system — is invisible to a derived sweep. That is not fatal, because the seam already answers it: `coverage_report` takes caller-supplied observations, so an agent that can reach a PLM or a document store sweeps it and hands the paths over exactly as it hands over a repo listing. Derivation is the DEFAULT, not a restriction on what may be observed. WHAT IS STILL OPEN AND WAS NEVER THIS: `cap:coverage` records that the sweep is not persisted, so `detect_gaps` cannot raise coverage from graph state the way `unresolved_drift` is raised from a recorded `DriftEvent`. That deferral survives this decision untouched — it was never the fix for the blind quadrant, and it still needs a node to record a sweep in and a staleness rule (the `cap:freshness` precedent).
properties.name: Coverage scope is DERIVED from version control — because a sweep covers the design's artifacts, never the subject system
properties.rationale: Anthony's word, given 2026-08-02 in answer to the three shapes put to him. Recorded with his argument rather than just his choice, because the argument is the part that would otherwise be lost: it is not merely a preference between three costs, it identifies an ERROR in how option 3 was described to him — the artifact/subject conflation — and that error is what would have made a later reader re-open a settled question. The two rejected shapes are kept in the record deliberately (ADR discipline): (1) a scope property on Project/Component, cheap but with no history and nowhere to date a sweep; (2) a first-class node recording a sweep and its scope, which would have closed the persistence deferral in the same move but costs a schema change and pulls in the staleness decision. Both remain available as an OVERRIDE for a subject version control cannot enumerate — this decision fixes the default, not the ceiling.
